Use the most recent information you know. Never invent figures: use null when unsure. Be specific (products, numbers, years).

Give each line one tag, the one that fits best)},

   (approximate latest fiscal-year figures for the company itself and for every listed competitor; decimals, e.g. 0.42; null if unknown),

                   "rows": [ {"name": "company name", "latest": decimal or null, "earlier": decimal or null} ] } ]  (up to 3 of its main markets, the company and its main rivals),
 "threats": ["specific things that could weaken its advantage"],
 "ceo": {"name": "current CEO", "founder": true or false, "since": "YYYY", "background": "e.g. electrical engineer, Stanford MBA"},

result.name: Berkshire Hathaway Inc.
result.industry: Diversified holding company (insurance, railroad, utilities, manufacturing, retail)
markets: Property and casualty insurance and reinsurance (GEICO, General Re, National Indemnity)
Electric and gas utilities and pipelines (Berkshire Hathaway Energy)
Industrial and consumer manufacturing (Precision Castparts, Lubrizol, Clayton Homes, OxyChem and others)
Truck stops and fuel (Pilot) and foodservice distribution (McLane)
Retailing and consumer brands (See's Candies, Dairy Queen, Duracell, auto dealers)
Public equity investing (Apple, American Express, Bank of America, Coca-Cola, Alphabet, Japanese trading houses)

mission.plain: Berkshire aims to grow its per-share value over the long run by owning good businesses outright or in part and keeping a very strong balance sheet.

about.plain: Berkshire Hathaway is a giant company that owns lots of other companies. It owns GEICO car insurance, the BNSF railroad, big power companies, Dairy Queen, See's Candies, Duracell batteries and many factories. It also owns shares in famous companies like Apple and Coca-Cola. Warren Buffett built it over 60 years, and Greg Abel now runs it.
about.customers: Millions of drivers, homeowners, businesses, utilities customers and shippers buy its insurance, power, freight and products.
about.everyday: If you have GEICO car insurance, ate a Dairy Queen Blizzard or used Duracell batteries, you have bought from Berkshire.

money.plain: car insurance (GEICO), business insurance and reinsurance, plus investment income on the float
aircraft parts, chemicals, building products, manufactured homes, batteries, clothing
delivers groceries and supplies to convenience stores and restaurants
Pilot truck stops, car dealers, furniture and jewelry stores, aviation services
electricity, natural gas and pipelines in the US and UK
moving freight by train across the western US

result.summary: Berkshire has a durable competitive advantage built on low-cost insurance float (about $176B at end-2025, earned at an 87.1% combined ratio in 2025), a fortress balance sheet with over $360B of cash and Treasuries, and a reputation that makes it the preferred buyer for family-owned businesses. Its operating businesses include wide-moat assets such as BNSF and GEICO, but its size limits growth, and the shift from Warren Buffett to Greg Abel in 2026 tests whether the capital-allocation edge survives.

pricingPower.evidence: GEICO raised auto rates sharply in 2023-2024, restoring underwriting margins (2025 insurance combined ratio 87.1%) though at the cost of policies in force and weaker retention; BNSF and the regulated utilities pass through price increases (BNSF operating margin rose to 34.5% in 2025), while See's Candies has raised prices almost every year for decades, but many manufacturing and retail units sell in competitive markets.

moats.evidence: Berkshire's reputation for integrity and permanent ownership makes it the buyer of choice for family firms, and it owns strong consumer brands such as GEICO, Dairy Queen, See's Candies and Duracell.
Auto insurance and most of its products can be switched easily; switching costs exist mainly for rail shippers on BNSF routes and utility customers.
Its businesses gain little from more users; BNSF's 32,500-mile network is a scale asset rather than a true network effect.

GEICO's direct-to-consumer model, BNSF's scale and Berkshire's ability to deploy float at near-zero or negative cost give it a structural cost-of-capital and operating cost advantage; it can write giant reinsurance risks few others can absorb.
BNSF is one of only two major western US railroads (with Union Pacific), and Berkshire Hathaway Energy's regulated utilities and pipelines operate as local monopolies.
Berkshire's decentralised model, refusal to sell acquired businesses and willingness to hold hundreds of billions in cash are hard for private equity or short-term-focused conglomerates to copy.

Disciplined underwriting culture in reinsurance (Ajit Jain's group) and a 60-year capital-allocation process have produced a 19.7% compounded annual gain in per-share market value from 1965 to 2025 versus 10.5% for the S&P 500.

Its roughly $176B insurance float and $370B+ cash pile at end-2025 are effectively exclusive capital resources; Warren Buffett's personal reputation was a cornered resource that is now transitioning to Greg Abel.

customers.evidence: Shareholders are famously loyal and the Omaha annual meeting draws tens of thousands, but at the operating level GEICO's customer retention fell in 2025 according to Greg Abel's shareholder letter, and BNSF has faced shipper service complaints.

talent.evidence: Berkshire retains founder-managers of acquired companies with an autonomy-based culture and has a tiny headquarters staff, but it pays modestly with no stock options and does not appear in major employer rankings.

product.evidence: Some holdings are best in class (BNSF, Precision Castparts in aerospace parts, General Re/National Indemnity in reinsurance), but GEICO lost ground to Progressive in auto-insurance telematics and pricing, and many subsidiaries are solid rather than category leaders.

threats: Loss of Warren Buffett's capital-allocation skill and reputation after Greg Abel became CEO on January 1, 2026
Sheer size: with about $750B of equity and $360B+ of cash, few acquisitions can move the needle, and cash earns falling Treasury yields
GEICO losing share to Progressive's superior telematics pricing, with retention falling in 2025
Large catastrophe losses (hurricanes, wildfires) and softening reinsurance pricing expected in 2026
Wildfire liability at PacifiCorp and regulatory pressure on Berkshire Hathaway Energy's utilities
Union Pacific's planned acquisition of Norfolk Southern creating a stronger transcontinental rail rival to BNSF
Concentrated equity portfolio (Apple, American Express, Bank of America, Coca-Cola) exposing earnings to market swings

ceo.name: Greg Abel
ceo.background: Chartered accountant (CPA), commerce degree from the University of Alberta; former PwC accountant who ran Berkshire Hathaway Energy and later all non-insurance operations as vice chairman

c1.evidence: Berkshire leads mature industries such as US auto insurance (GEICO is No. 3), western freight rail (BNSF) and utilities, not a fast-growing emerging industry.

c2.evidence: Sellers of family businesses choose Berkshire for permanent ownership and autonomy, and policyholders and reinsurance clients value its unmatched financial strength; these are rooted in 60 years of reputation and a $370B+ cash pile that are very hard to copy.

c3.evidence: Berkshire and Warren Buffett are household names, it is the default example of long-term value investing, and GEICO is one of the most recognised insurance brands in America.

c4.evidence: Berkshire publishes no formal mission statement, but its Owner's Manual and decentralised values of integrity and long-term ownership, reaffirmed in Greg Abel's first annual letter for 2025, are consistently emphasised and management is famously not motivated by pay (Buffett took $100,000 a year).

c5.evidence: Shippers relying on BNSF, millions of utility and GEICO customers and the businesses it rescued in crises (e.g. Goldman Sachs and Bank of America) would notice, but most of its products could be replaced by competitors.

c6.evidence: “Warren Buffett, trustworthy, value investing, cash pile” – the public impression is overwhelmingly positive, built on Buffett's reputation for integrity and long-term results.

c7.evidence: Its markets (insurance, rail, utilities, manufacturing) are huge, and utilities benefit from rising power demand from data centers, but most of its businesses grow at roughly GDP rates rather than riding a secular trend.

c8.evidence: As a holding company with $360B+ of cash and Treasuries in mid-2026 it can enter almost any industry by acquisition, as shown by the OxyChem purchase in 2025 and Taylor Morrison homebuilding in 2026.

m1.evidence: Greg Abel is respected as a disciplined operator who built Berkshire Hathaway Energy, but he is not known for a bold vision of the future beyond preserving Berkshire's model.

m2.evidence: Abel is not a founder but has worked within Berkshire for over 25 years, owns substantial Berkshire stock and is focused on keeping the company going for decades, in Buffett's founder-like tradition.

m4.evidence: Berkshire's model of trusting subsidiary CEOs with autonomy is supportive of managers, but there is little public evidence on Abel's servant-leadership style with front-line employees and customers.

m5.evidence: Berkshire has a strong, distinctive culture of decentralisation, integrity and frugality built by Buffett, but it is designed for capital allocation and stewardship rather than inventing new products and technologies.

m6.evidence: Abel is known for being deeply hands-on with Berkshire's operating businesses, but he is an accountant by training, not an engineer, and Berkshire is not a technology company.

m7.evidence: Abel is regarded as having strong integrity, and Berkshire's stewardship continues Buffett's pledge to give over 99% of his fortune to philanthropy, though Abel's own record as CEO is still short.

m7b.evidence: No record was found of Greg Abel giving a commencement speech at a top university.

m8b.evidence: Greg Abel is seen as low-key and private, in contrast to Warren Buffett's famous folksy personality.

m9.evidence: Abel grew Berkshire Hathaway Energy from MidAmerican into a utility empire and, as vice chairman for non-insurance operations, oversaw businesses earning record operating profits; Berkshire's 2025 operating earnings were $44.5B and Q2 2026 operating earnings rose 16% to $13.0B.

m10.evidence: Berkshire is famous for frugality: a headquarters of about two dozen people in Omaha, Buffett's modest house and salary, and no corporate jet culture for the parent company.

c10.evidence: Its railroad, utilities, insurance and manufacturing quietly serve hundreds of millions of people, but it does not transform lives the way a breakthrough consumer technology does.

p2.evidence: Building a 60-year record of compounding capital at about 19.7% a year is extraordinarily hard, and BNSF and its utilities are critical infrastructure, but most of its individual businesses are not technologically hard to replicate.

f1.evidence: Revenue rose every year from $245.5B in 2020 to $371.4B in 2024, then was flat at $371.4B in 2025.

f2.evidence: Berkshire does not report a consolidated gross or operating margin; operating earnings rose from $21.9B in 2020 to $47.4B in 2024 before slipping to $44.5B in 2025, which implies a higher earnings margin than five years ago.

f3.evidence: At June 30, 2026 Berkshire held about $365B of cash and Treasury bills versus about $129B of borrowings (most of it non-recourse debt at BNSF and BHE), with $748B of shareholders' equity.

f4.evidence: Operating earnings roughly doubled from $21.9B in 2020 to $47.4B in 2024 but fell to $44.5B in 2025, and operating cash flow rose over the period, though with year-to-year swings.

v1.evidence: Berkshire is a holding company with no single main product; GEICO, its best-known consumer product, is not clearly better than Progressive or State Farm for an ordinary buyer.

v2.evidence: Berkshire is admired by investors (it ranks highly in Fortune's World's Most Admired Companies), but it is not on major best-employer lists such as Fortune's 100 Best Companies to Work For.
